data.title: Ex-GOP strategist: 'This might be the year' Democrats win Texas
data.description:
Former GOP strategist Joseph Moreno said “this might be the year” that Democrats win in Texas after a three-decade drought since a Democrat has won in the Lone Star State.

In an appearance on CNN’s “The Lead,” host Jake Tapper asked Moreno about recent polling that showed Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D-Texas) leading Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) 47 percent to 45 percent.

“It surprises me, and it worries me a little bit, Jake. Normally, I would say, ‘I’m not worried about this,’ right? It’s been 30 years since a Democrat won statewide office in Texas,” Moreno said.

Paxton won a primary runoff against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) earlier this year with the help of an endorsement from President Trump.

Talarico won the Democratic primary against Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D) in March and received heavy support from Democratic leadership including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

“The problem is, here’s what happens — in 2024, the Republican was up by 2 percent, wins by 8 percent. In 2020, Cornyn was up 10 percent, wins by 10 percent,” Moreno continued. “Now, you’ve got Talarico even, or maybe even ahead of Paxton. Paxton is so flawed. I’m embarrassed as a Republican.”

Paxton faced scrutiny from Texas state officials following a state House investigation that found he had “used, misused, or failed to use his official powers in a manner calculated to subvert the lawful operation of the government.”

He also was impeached by the Texas House, faces 20 charges of misconduct in office, previously faced three felony securities fraud charges and had an extramarital affair.

A Texas Pulse/Texas A&M Bush School poll released Friday had 47 percent of likely Texas voters planning to support Talarico, while 43 percent chose Paxton.

“I hate to say it, this might be the year for Democrats in Texas,” Moreno concluded.

The general election between Paxton and Talarico happens on Nov. 3.

data.title: What happens when progressives stop reproducing?
data.description:
The U.S. General Social Survey has tracked American life since 1972. Its findings reveal a pattern that political consultants have largely ignored.

The deep division in national politics is no longer an ideological battle over tax codes and foreign policy. Rather, it’s a battle of the bedrooms. Left-leaning Americans are averaging far fewer children than conservatives, whose birth rates hold steady near the 2.1 replacement level.

Evolutionary demographers Martin Fieder and Susanne Huber recently pinpointed the precise moment this divergence began. For Americans born before 1943, political leanings showed little correlation with family size. The baby boom was an equal-opportunity event. But for those born after 1943, political ideology became a reliable predictor of family size.

As the researchers note, higher education accelerates this divide. Women now earn 58 percent of all bachelor’s degrees, and university campuses tilt heavily toward progressive politics. This extended academic timeline delays marriage, trading early family formation for career building. The campus functions as an ideological funnel, leaving the highest-scoring students on standardized tests with the lowest reproductive rates. Academics have engineered a bizarre biological paradox: the most credentialed segment of society is choosing genetic extinction, leaving the future to the children of subcultures that skip the university pipeline entirely.

Political parties invest billions in media campaigns to win over independent voters. Demography operates by simple math, counting the actual humans entering the world. Frequent religious attendance remains the primary engine of conservative fertility. Churches provide strong social infrastructure, offering communal childcare, moral validation, and structured matchmaking. In such an environment, raising four children changes from an expensive luxury hobby into an absolute cosmic obligation.

This reproductive advantage compounds over generations through family retention. Pew Research Center data confirms that children raised in highly religious, conservative households overwhelmingly maintain those exact beliefs into adulthood. Ideology functions like a heritable trait. When a culture passes down both its metaphysical worldview and its high-fertility habits, it unlocks exponential demographic interest. The devout always claim that Jesus saves, but in this specific instance, he also populates.

Progressive philosophies face no dramatic defeat at the ballot box. They require no cancelation by rivals and no losses in public debate. They are simply running out of citizens. A political movement that fails to reproduce automatically surrenders its institutional real estate to the descendants of the people who fill church pews instead of university lecture halls.

Conventional political analysts obsess over changing party platforms and legislative gridlock. The real driver of history is a profound divide in foundational attitudes toward permanent obligations. One mindset treats cultural continuity as life’s primary goal. The alternative prioritizes personal autonomy, geographic mobility, and self-definition above generational replacement.

Fieder and Huber isolate these metrics with rather unsexy statistics. Decades of low birth rates systematically warp the age profile of a nation. Roads, bridges and power grids built for a growing society become impossible to maintain when the tax base shrinks. Domestic economies become structurally addicted to foreign immigration to keep factory floors running and eldercare facilities staffed.

National debates focus on quarterly productivity figures, economic slowdowns and media polarization. Meanwhile, the biological reality of reproduction runs in the background. Differential reproduction operates completely outside the 24-hour news cycle. Certain belief structures maintain compatibility with biological survival over centuries, while others act as demographic sterilizers. Societies survive political volatility quite easily; they do not survive long-term reproductive deficits.

Building a nation of genuine worth requires citizens to view family formation as a primary objective. This outlook belongs almost exclusively to traditional communities that view children as central duties rather than limits on personal freedom. Macro-level cultural shifts are merely the sum of millions of private decisions, including the mattress-testing ones, made over decades. By the time a nation notices its declining birth rate, the concrete has already set.

The survival of any political philosophy relies on its submission to basic reproductive reality. American economic dominance requires a baseline population to secure domestic supply chains, staff military branches and drive innovation.

This continuity relies on a classic form of conservatism — entirely distinct from populist trends or immediate election cycles — built on the absolute conviction that a society has a duty to reproduce itself. It demands a mindset that rejects the idea of a terminal generation, viewing children as an existential necessity and the ultimate justification for a nation’s existence.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

data.title: How does cyclospora compare to some of the worst outbreaks in US history?
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Amid the ongoing investigations into outbreaks of both “explosive diarrhea”-causing cyclospora and salmonella affecting dozens of states, the daily headlines are reminiscent of past foodborne illness crises that gripped the nation.

As of August 4, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported that there have been 10,468 lab-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis since May 1, including those tied to Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce sourced from Mexico.

The CDC says there have been more than 12,255 unconfirmed cases, many of which were reported in Michigan, where two people have died.

Meantime, jalapeño peppers – also sourced from Mexico – have been linked to at least 345 cases of salmonella across 27 states. At least three dozen people have been hospitalized, with the outbreak prompting major Mexican food chains Chipotle and Qdoba to pull jalapeños from their menus.

Despite the widespread publicity and thousands of cases involved, the two current outbreaks have so far proven less deadly than some historic, notorious cases.

Contaminated oysters lead to typhoid outbreak (1924)

Oysters contaminated with Salmonella Typhi led to a deadly outbreak of typhoid fever in 1924 that killed 150 people and sickened an estimated 1,500, according to Michigan State University researchers.

Those who died may have been ill for up to three weeks, left “delirious or lying motionless from exhaustion, eyes half closed in what is called ‘the typhoid state,'” according to one report.

The tainted oysters were believed to have been distributed by a company in West Sayville, New York. It was the deadliest outbreak in U.S. history and led to the creation of National Shellfish Sanitation Program.

Mexican-style cheese (1985)

The outbreak, centered in Los Angeles County, was believed to have been caused by tainted, unpasteurized milk used to make soft Mexican cheese.

Of the 142 cases, more than half were pregnant women or their children. According to a report in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), 28 people died, including 18 adults and 10 newborns.

Investigators ultimately traced the outbreak to cheeses made by Jalisco Mexican Projects Inc.

Jack in the Box (1992-1993)

An outbreak of E. coli killed four children in four states and sickened more than 700 people across Washington, Idaho, California and Nevada before investigators finally traced it to undercooked hamburgers sold at Jack in the Box.

The ensuing investigation by federal regulators changed regulatory practices in the U.S., experts say.

An investigation by the CDC identified five slaughter plants in the U.S. and one in Canada as the likely sources of animals used in the contaminated lots of meat and identified potential control points for reducing the likelihood of contamination. The animals slaughtered in domestic slaughter plants were traced to farms and auctions in six western states. No one slaughter plant or farm was identified as the source.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture mandated a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point system, which helps identify and control hazards within the system of food production. The system provided for more monitoring and controls to rapidly limit the spread of outbreaks.

Schwan’s ice cream (1994)

A nationwide salmonella outbreak that sickened an estimated 224,000 people in 1994 was caused by ice cream from Minnesota-based Schwan’s Company.

Investigators determined that the source of the salmonella was the tanker trailers that transported the pasteurized ice cream premix. Those same trailers previously carried non-pasteurized liquid eggs that tested positive for the bacteria, according to a study published by the National Library of Medicine.

E. coli outbreak in spinach (2006)

A 2006 outbreak of E. coli traced to contaminated fresh spinach infected 199 people across 26 states, according to the CDC. Three people died, including a 2-year-old.

After speaking with patients, some of whom still had the spinach bags in their homes, federal investigators identified the source of the contamination as a load of spinach grown on a field in California adjacent to land used for cattle grazing, according to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Samples of river water taken as close as one mile away from the spinach were found to be contaminated with E. coli, as were samples of cattle and wild pig feces from the ranch.

Peanut butter (2008-09)

Peanut butter tainted with salmonella killed nine people and sickened hundreds, leading to a 28-year prison sentence for the former CEO of the Peanut Corporation of America, Stewart Parnell.

An indictment said the company misled its customers about the existence of salmonella in its product, even when lab tests showed it was present. It added that the co-workers even fabricated certificates accompanying some of the peanut shipments saying they were safe when tests said otherwise.

A jury convicted Parnell of 71 counts including conspiracy, obstruction of justice, wire fraud and other crimes related to the salmonella outbreak in 2008 and 2009.

It prompted one of the largest food recalls in U.S. history.

Contaminated cantaloupes (2011)

Two farmers were charged and convicted in a listeriosis outbreak that left 33 dead and sickened another 147, according to the CDC.

The tainted cantaloupes came from Jensen Farms in Holly, Colorado.

The owners of the farmer, Eric and Ryan Jensen, were accused of failing to wash the melons properly, leading to the nationwide outbreak. They were both given five years of probation.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Sam Alito is locked and loaded for another term
data.description:
A month after National Public Radio’s Nina Totenberg announced that Sam Alito was retiring (a story NPR later had to retract), the 76-year-old jurist told the Wall Street Journal in an interview, “Obviously, I’m here for another term.”

Looking at the docket for the coming term, it is easy to see why. Even after overturning Roe v. Wade and other historic opinions, Alito still has unfinished business. An example can be found in two cases involving bans on semiautomatic rifles like the AR-15 that are now awaiting argument in the October term.

Many of us have been frustrated by the Court’s failure to address these laws barring AR-15s and other weapons. Just last year, the Supreme Court declined review of such a Maryland law. Alito and Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch indicated that they wanted to hear the case, failing just one vote short of granting certiorari.

Notably, the required fourth vote could have come from Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who called the Fourth Circuit’s ruling in Snope v. Brown “questionable” and added that the Court “should and presumably will address the AR-15 issue soon, in the next Term or two.”

Now, it will.

Democrats are moving in various states to ban the nation’s most popular rifle (the AR-15) and its most popular handgun (the semiautomatic 9mm). Some of us view these laws as presumptively unconstitutional.

In 2008, the court declared in its opinion in Heller that gun ownership is an individual right. The court emphasized how these weapons were in common use and not the type of dangerous or unusual weapon that would fall outside of the Second Amendment. Handguns, the opinion reads, “are the most popular weapon chosen by Americans for self-defense in the home, and a complete prohibition of their use is invalid.”

In 2022, the Court held in the Bruen case that the government bears the burden of demonstrating that any restriction upon the right to keep and bear arms “is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

The bans on Glock handguns and semiautomatic rifles are efforts to achieve indirectly what the Supreme Court barred directly. In Virginia, Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) immediately moved against gun rights after her election. Ironically, her election not only spurred a massive surge in gun purchases, but she then supplied the lead line of briefs challenging the law. Spanberger admitted that the state law she signed would ban commonly used hunting guns.

In what is known as the court’s “clean-up conference,” the justices granted review in Illinois and Connecticut cases challenging bans on semiautomatic rifles.

In Viramontes v. Cook County, the Seventh Circuit relied on an earlier ruling that gun owners had failed to show “that the covered firearms materially differed from machine guns and military-grade weaponry, which the Supreme Court instructed can be banned under the Second Amendment.”

In Grant v. Higgins, the Second Circuit upheld a similar ban after agreeing with the state that the law imposes “a burden comparable to historical antecedents that regulated other unusually dangerous weapons unsuitable for and disproportionate to the objective of individual self-defense.”

Notably, in the Illinois case, Cook County argued that these are not just unusually dangerous weapons, but that the challengers cannot offer “even a single instance in which assault weapons were ever used in lawful self-defense.”

That is a highly dubious claim. Since 1990, there have been an estimated 32,091,000 Modern Sporting Rifles in circulation. These are semiautomatic models, which means they fire a single bullet and then automatically load another cartridge into the chamber. The AR-15 is the most popular model, and there are estimates that it has as many as 25 million owners.

The popularity of the AR-15 is due to the fact that it is modular, with some models allowing one to swap out barrels, bolts and high-capacity magazines, or add a variety of accessories. It is also not the most powerful gun; many guns have equal or greater calibers.

There is roughly the same number of Glock pistols in circulation. That means perhaps 40 million Americans currently possess weapons that Democrats are trying to ban as unusually dangerous and completely unprotected.

With the granting of these cases, Virginia’s ban on new sales of the AR-15 rifle and other guns will have to await the final decisions. 

These gun bans are not the only cases involving politically popular, legally dubious legislation. The first case to be argued will be Suncor Energy v. Commissioners of Boulder County, a challenge to state laws imposing damages on fossil fuel companies for climate change.

With a docket like that, one can see why Alito is not going anywhere.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: After detainee's death, New Jersey to investigate ICE facility
data.description:
New Jersey is launching a civil rights investigation into Delaney Hall, the state’s largest immigration detention facility, following reports of poor conditions and deaths, state officials announced Friday.

The New Jersey Division on Civil Rights issued subpoenas involving the center, privately owned by GEO Group, to examine whether its staff violated detainees’ civil rights — alleging inhumane treatment and failure to provide proper medical care.

“New Jersey has a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people in our State,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in a statement. “We ask individuals to share their personal experiences with us so that we can take action to ensure that rights are protected.”

The probe comes days after Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a 41-year-old Salvadorian man, died after suffering a “medical emergency” while being detained at Delaney Hall. His family claimed the facility did not allow him consistent access to medication used to treat his ongoing health conditions.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed the cause of death as cardiac arrest but claimed the detainee had “no medical records of cardiac problems.“

Mullin added that Lopez Cornejo was on a diet and given medication for his hypertension and diabetes diagnoses.

Davenport’s office said it could also pursue civil enforcement action under state law if the investigation uncovers violations committed by the facility and by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) said the investigation was a “necessary course of action” after accusing the facility of “stonewalling efforts for real oversight.”

The Sherrill administration sued the GEO Group in June after alleging state health inspectors were blocked from accessing the facility.

“We will not tolerate a facility that abdicates any transparency and accountability. I have long opposed private detention facilities, and my position is clear that Delaney Hall should be closed,” Sherrill said in a statement Friday. “My administration will continue to do everything in our power to hold ICE and The GEO Group accountable to New Jersey laws.”

data.title: Hunter Biden acknowledges pardon was likely 'not good' for father's legacy
data.description:
Hunter Biden, the son of former President Biden, on Friday said the pardon he received in 2024 was “not good” for the American people or his father’s legacy, calling himself the “the most privileged person there is.”

The younger Biden, in an interview with BBC’s “Newsnight,” said he understood the backlash the former president received after issuing the clemency, after he repeatedly pledged that he would not intervene in his son’s criminal cases.

“It’s something that is easily criticized and for good reason,” Hunter told the outlet. “It’s not fair.”

“I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it: my father,” he added.

Hunter noted he was “eternally grateful” for the privilege from his father, because he believed President Trump’s incoming administration would have retaliated against him for revenge against his “political enemies.” Still, he acknowledged the risks.

“Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my father’s legacy? No on all counts,” he continued.

Biden granted his son clemency covering federal offenses Hunter committed or may have committed between Jan. 1, 2014, and Dec. 1, 2024. The pardon wiped away Hunter’s federal gun conviction and tax charges to which he pleaded guilty to.

In a statement announcing the pardon, the former president argued his son had been “selectively, and unfairly, prosecuted.”

“I hope Americans will understand why a father and a President would come to this decision,” Biden said at the time.

Hunter told the BBC that the two never discussed the possibility of a pardon before his father, who has been battling a cancer diagnosis, granted it.

“There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public,” he added.

data.title: Saharan dust cloud the size of the continental US is impacting summer weather and you may not have even noticed
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – The days are hot. The storms are few and far between. The sunsets are beautiful. And high in the sky is a layer of dust that has traveled thousands of miles from Africa impacting the weather we’re seeing in the southern U.S. and beyond.

The Saharan Air Layer, often referred to as Saharan dust, is a 2.5-mile thick “layer cake” that starts about a mile up in the atmosphere, explained Jason Dunion, a University of Miami meteorologist who works closely with NOAA’s Hurricane Research Division.

“They roll off of Africa in the summertime every three to five days, and they’re huge. They’re about the size of the lower 48 states as they cross the Atlantic,” Dunion said.

The Saharan dust season usually peaks between mid-June and mid-August and it’s currently impacting weather around the U.S. in ways you may not have even realized. The layer of warm, dry, dusty air tends to break up the development of thunderstorms and hurricanes.

“It really helps to cap the atmosphere,” said Dunion. “It makes it very hard for thunderstorms and clouds to break that really warm layer.”

It’s one reason we may be seeing such a quiet start to the Atlantic hurricane season.

“Look at this late-season plume. That is healthy,” meteorologist Rebecca Barry at Nexstar’s WFLA said while showing a map of the Saharan dust plume. “That looks like a late-May or June plume of Saharan dust. … It is pretty rare that this late in the season we have such a healthy plume of Saharan dust breaking off from the coastline of Africa and moving across the Atlantic.”

All that dust can prevent storm formation, including tropical depressions that would otherwise turn into tropical storms and hurricanes as they head toward the U.S.

Without as many summer storms, the temperature has been rising in the South. “We don’t really get those cool afternoon thunderstorms that we usually get when we’ve got these dust outbreaks overhead. So they tend to be in the hottest days of the year, and we’ve had heat indexes getting up to 110,” said Dunion.

Even beyond the South and Gulf states, the dust is having an impact. KXAN meteorologist Freddy Vela showed back-to-back waves of Saharan dust sweeping across Texas and as far west as Arizona in a forecast this week.

Another side-effect of the Saharan Air Layer: spectacular sunrises and sunsets. As the dust washes over Florida, it scatters the light and can create an orange glow at dawn and dusk.

“To me, it’s amazing,” said Dunion. “It’s traveled 3,000, 4,000 miles across the Atlantic bu you can still see it.”

data.title: Enes Kanter Freedom declares for 2027 WNBA Draft
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom has declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft.

Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA before he was waived by the Houston Rockets in February 2022.

The former basketball star is listed as 6 foot 10 inches and 250 pounds on his NBA player profile. His desire to play in the league follows controversy amongst some players, several of whom have welcomed transgender women to be part of a WNBA team.

Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham has become the poster child for the debate after telling ESPN her thoughts on transgender women in women’s sports.

“After careful consideration and reviewing the current eligibility guidelines, I’m officially declaring myself a @WNBA prospect,” Freedom announced on social platform X. “If simply declaring who you are is all that’s required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA.”

“My team and I have carefully examined the WNBA’s eligibility criteria and governing framework surrounding self-identification and inclusion,” he added in the post. “Based on the current guidelines, I can and am officially declaring my eligibility for the upcoming WNBA draft in April 2027.”

“I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices, the athlete continued. “I’m simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone — the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for.”

Freedom noted that he and his team want to see the guidelines “applied equally, consistently, and without exception.”

The Women’s National Basketball Players Association released a statement following Freedom’s announcement.

“We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion. Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change,” the statement read.

“Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations,” the group added in the Instagram post. “But we will not be used as political pawns.”

Last month, Freedom told NewsNation that Caitlin Clark’s Fever teammates, and the WNBA more broadly, need to do more to protect the face of the league.

data.title: Supporting Israel isn't charity — it's America's best weapon
data.description:
America needs a tough, capable ally right now — not a fair-weather friend, not a country that ghosts us the moment things get hard.

Israel is that ally. No nation on Earth matches its military muscle, intelligence reach, technological edge, combat experience and sheer will to fight.

The recent war proved it. John Hannah, a former national security adviser to Vice President Dick Cheney, called the U.S.-Israel military partnership “a qualitative leap forward.” This isn’t a handshake deal. It is a battle-tested alliance that delivers results in real time. 

And the enemy it delivers against is Iran, the world’s top exporter of terrorism. 

Iran’s regime is a fanatical machine that crushes its own people to fund chaos abroad. The way it treats women is not a side-issue — it is the regime’s playbook. A regime that subjugates half of its population isn’t just wasting talent. It is teaching domination as doctrine: obedience over freedom, force over persuasion. That doctrine doesn’t stay at home; it is Iran’s chief global export. 

Tehran has chosen repression, torture and slaughter over prosperity. Oil money that could build schools instead bankrolls Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis — terrorist proxy militias spreading misery from Gaza to the Arabian Sea.

The Houthis have already choked off shipping lanes. Iran doesn’t even need to fully shut the Strait of Hormuz, since the mere threat is enough to spike insurance costs and gas prices from Ohio to Osaka.

If we stop short of finishing the job in Iran, its regime walks away with its uranium intact, its missiles intact and a stranglehold on global oil. Weakness, to Tehran, is an invitation to continue to terrorize the Middle East and possibly the free world. 

This is why Israel matters. It built its military, intelligence and tech edge because its survival demanded it. And unlike some allies, it still has the guts to use it. Britain used to play this role, but decades of budget cuts and lost nerve have ended that. Nobody else brings what Israel brings.

Some American politicians are cheering for the wrong side. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has at times vowed to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu the moment he lands in New York, despite having zero legal authority to do it. His dangerous stunt only tells Iran and its terror network that politics might succeed where bombs have failed in splitting America from its strongest ally.

Netanyahu himself called it out for what it is. On Fox News, he said Mamdani was “fomenting hate” and turning New Yorkers against each other, and he is right. A sitting mayor spending his political capital boasting about the unlikely arrest of a foreign head of state, rather than the safety of his own constituents, isn’t leadership; it is theater with a target on someone’s back. 

And Mamdani’s isn’t some fringe temper tantrum — over 100 House Democrats already voted to cut off military financing for Israel.

The fix is straightforward, if overdue: Stop treating this alliance like a handout. No other partner brings Israel’s combination of firepower, intelligence and tech innovation. That is the case for retiring the word “aid” and building a real partnership in its place. 

Direct financial assistance can shrink as the alliance gets deeper — joint research, shared weapons programs, intelligence sharing, coordinated planning on AI, missile defense, cyber warfare and quantum computing. This is not about scaling back. It’s about leveling up. 

It is smart politics, too. As long as this relationship runs through “aid,” critics on both sides will keep painting Israel as a freeloader instead of what it actually is: a battle-tested partner that makes America safer.

Make that shift, and you kill the argument being used to tear this alliance apart. Israel stays indispensable — but everyone finally sees the relationship for what it is: an investment, not a handout. 

This isn’t charity, it’s national security. 

Iran offers fanaticism, repression and chaos. Israel offers strength, innovation and the will to fight back. America must stand with Israel and deny Iran its win. Let’s finish the job.

Earle Mack is a former U.S. ambassador to Finland.

data.title: Live updates: Senate departs for August recess; Blanche confirmed as AG
data.description:
Senators wrapped up a busy final stretch of work early Saturday, confirming Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department (DOJ) and passing a stopgap funding bill before adjourning for the August recess.

Blanche, President Trump’s former personal attorney, has served as acting attorney general since April and was confirmed in a narrow 50-49 vote. Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) joined Democrats in opposing his nomination.

The continuing resolution will shift the government shutdown deadline to Dec. 11.

Other GOP priorities were left unfinished as lawmakers depart Washington, likely setting up another packed agenda when they return.

Meanwhile, Trump is facing fresh questions about the economy heading into the fall. A weaker-than-expected July jobs report on Friday showed employers cutting 23,000 jobs, as rising inflation and affordability dominate voters’ concerns ahead of the midterm elections.

Follow live below.
